s02.title: Introduction
sentences: Today I want to talk about FluOLinGo.
That’s capital F, O, L and G, and it stands for Fluency On Linguistic Goals.
It’s a platform for beginners learning French, and I built it myself, with no coding background and no development team.

s03.title: What I mean by goals
sentences: As the name suggests, the whole thing is organised around goals.
I call them goals, but they’re really what teachers know as learning objectives.
And the communicative goals are much like what ACTFL calls can-do statements.
voice: As the name suggests, the whole thing is organised around goals.
I call them goals, but they’re really what teachers know as learning objectives.
And the communicative goals are much like what ACTFL calls can-do statements.

s04.title: Two kinds of goals
sentences: In the 1970s, the applied linguist David Wilkins argued that a syllabus should cover the meanings and functions learners need to express, alongside the grammar.
FluOLinGo uses both.
Linguistic goals are about the language itself.
Communicative goals are about what you do with it, like saying what you like or inviting a friend out.
Later frameworks, like the CEFR, went further and distinguished between sounds, vocabulary, grammar and writing.
In this talk, I split grammar into two: word forms, like verb endings, and sentence structure, like word order.
So I end up with five types of linguistic goal: sounds, vocabulary, word forms, sentence structure and script.

s05.title: The question and the plan
sentences: Wilkins was working on a framework for European languages.
But could the same principles work for a language as different as Chinese?
That’s the question I want to look at today.
Can a platform built for French work for Chinese, a language that’s so different?
And if so, what can stay the same, and what has to change?
I’ll start with the French course, then look at what makes Chinese different.
I’ll show you how the same approach can be adapted, using examples from both textbooks, and finish with some steps you can try with your own language.

s06.title: From fifty goals that all looked alike to three kinds of step
sentences: This is where FluOLinGo began.
It teaches beginner French using our course book, L’Atelier.
In the first version, I cut the course into fifty small goals across five units and laid them out on a map.
That’s the left side of the slide: fifty numbered goals in a row.
Every exercise belonged to a goal.
In other words, I started with the goal, then built the exercises around it.
But look at three of those goals.
Number twenty-eight, negation, is linguistic.
Number twenty-nine, inviting someone and turning down an invitation, is communicative.
Number thirty, writing an email, is a whole task.
On the map, though, all three looked exactly the same: one stop each.
And that was a problem, because they are not the same kind of thing.
Negation is one small building block.
Writing an email is a whole piece of work that needs many of those blocks.
So a learner moving along the map could not tell a small step from a big one, or see which goals the email depended on.
At first, I didn’t notice this, because I was simply following the French book, which already sorts its content into situations and tasks.
But when I started planning the Chinese version, that support was gone.
The Chinese book has no situations and no tasks at all.
That meant I had to decide, for every step, what kind of step it was.
And that is when I saw that the map was mixing three different kinds.
On the right is the revised structure.
Each unit now has two kinds of goal, linguistic and communicative, and one task at the end, where learners use both together.
And you’ll see that same structure in both languages.

s07.title: One lesson page per linguistic goal
sentences: Each linguistic goal gets its own lesson page.
Communicative goals, on the other hand, get something different: four activities, one each for listening, reading, speaking and writing.
I’ll show you those shortly.
Sometimes, though, one stop brings in more than one concept, in the same lesson.
In Unit 0, for example, the days of the week come together with the moments of the day: morning and evening, for instance.
That’s because beginners need both from the very first lesson, and because they overlap: you say “Monday morning” in one breath.
Each page has six tabs.
Learners start with the course path, then move through explanations, forms and exercises, with bonus material and a word list at the end.
Let’s look more closely at one of those tabs.
Here is the exercise tab of another page, for “to like”.
It is a single sentence generator with three levels.
Each sentence starts from pictures: for example, “we”, a broken heart and a piano.
At one star, the verb is given, and you pick its right form from a list of all its forms.

And after that, the Bonus gives you the English and asks for the French, with no help at all.
So what I learned here: one exercise, three levels.
Keep it on one page, with one generator.
That’s it.

s08.title: Each unit: linguistic goals, situations, one task
sentences: Each unit combines linguistic goals and communicative goals, which L’Atelier calls situations.
As we’ve just seen, each linguistic goal gets a lesson page, while each situation represents something learners can do with the language.
Sometimes, however, the book packs several things into one situation.
When it does, I split them up, so each situation has one purpose.
But how do the two kinds fit together?
They meet in a grid.
Linguistic goals go down the side, and situations go across the top.
Here’s part of Unit 2, for example.
“To like the” helps you say what you like, and also say why.
Negation, for its part, turns up in several situations at once.
In other words, one linguistic goal can serve lots of situations, and one situation can need lots of linguistic goals.
So with the grid, I can see at a glance what a learner needs before tackling each situation.

This actually brings together two approaches Wilkins talked about: building language up piece by piece, which is the synthetic approach, and starting with what learners need to do, which is the analytic approach.
Later, Janice Yalden called something similar a proportional syllabus, bringing structure and communication together.
Finally, every unit finishes with one task that uses all its situations.
L’Atelier calls it the Mission.
All in all, in the new plan, the French course has thirty-seven situations and around sixty linguistic goals.

s09.title: Saying what you like: French Unit 2
sentences: Let me take one situation from start to finish, so you can see how it all fits.
We’re in French Unit 2.
The situation is saying what you like.
You can see the French title here.
First, learners work through the linguistic goals using the three-star progression and Bonus you’ve just seen.
On the left is the exercise tab from my original page.
Once they have the language they need, learners practise the situation in four different ways.
In ÉcouTexte, they listen to it.
Next, in G-Compris, which means “I understood,” they read a short everyday document, like the message on the right, and answer questions that check what the course has actually taught.

s11.title: Where French and Chinese put the weight
sentences: Chinese has no articles and no verb conjugations.
Instead, what it does have is measure words, aspect markers and tones.
But you can still use the same five categories for both languages.
In fact, I’d argue they work for any language.
What changes is how important each one is.
Let’s start with what the two languages share.
French and Mandarin overlap on vocabulary and sentence structure.
Both use subject, verb, object.
For example, look at these two sentences: “I go skiing” and “I drink coffee.” They’re built almost the same way.
Beyond that, though, they divide the work differently.
In French, word endings do a lot of the work.
In Chinese, by contrast, sounds and vocabulary matter much more, and word order does a lot of the grammatical work.
So let’s go through the five categories, one by one.
First, sounds, which carry a huge amount of weight.
Tones matter from the very first day, because if you get the tone wrong, you’ve said a different word.
Look at this example: one syllable in four tones.
Mother, hemp, horse, scold.
Four separate words.
So while in French a pronunciation mistake usually gets forgiven, in Chinese a tone mistake often won’t.
Second, vocabulary, which is another big challenge.
For one thing, there are almost no cognates to help you.
And because of the characters, every word has to be learned twice: once by ear and once in writing.
Third, word forms, on the other hand, are much simpler.
For example, aspect particles do some of the work that tense endings do in French, without the conjugation tables.
Fourth, sentence structure, by contrast, matters enormously.
Because Chinese has little inflection, grammar relies on word order, topic and comment, and particles.
Look at the pair of sentences here.
It’s a classic example.
And here’s something interesting.
Measure words give Chinese its own kind of agreement.
In French, every noun has a gender, and the article and adjective have to match it.
In Chinese, in the same way, every noun has its own classifier.
Here you’ve got a photo, a bottle and a room, and each takes a different one.
So you basically have to learn the classifier along with the noun.
In short, Chinese has plenty of grammar.
It’s just moved out of the word endings and into the vocabulary and the sentence.
Fifth and last, writing is a different story altogether.
For Chinese, it’s a whole track of its own.
But some languages, including many Indigenous languages, are learned mostly by listening, so they have few script goals, or none.

s12.title: Frame, slots, settings
s12.part: Part 3 · Moving the template to Chinese
sentences: So how do I take what I’ve built for French and adapt it to Chinese?
I do it in three steps.
Step one: keep the frame.
In other words, build the parts that work for any language just once.
There are also two important rules built into it: the catalogue and the spiral.
I’ll come to those in a moment.
Step two: change the settings.
That means the exercises still work the same way, but learners make different choices.
Step three: fill the slots.
That means using the new textbook to work out what learners need to be able to do.
And this third step is where the teacher does the real work.
To picture it, think of a loom.
The loom stays the same.
That’s the frame.
But the thread and pattern change with each language.
Now let’s take the steps one at a time.

s13.title: The frame: built once, filled twice
sentences: Let’s start with step one.
The frame is simply everything I can reuse, whatever language I’m teaching.

That includes the lesson pages, four types of exercise for sentences, words, set phrases and sounds, the different difficulty levels, bonus material, situation activities, unit tasks and the learning map.
So for Chinese, the activities keep their structure, but the texts and words change.
On top of that, there’s one more thing, and I actually only finalised it this week: the catalogue.
The rule is simple: never teach or test anything the book doesn’t cover.
To make sure of that, I’ve designed the site to check that catalogue in four different places.
First, there’s a check that stops the site from building anything beyond the course limits.
Then there’s the path tab on each lesson, a page for each unit, and the search.
For example, type the French word for “midnight,” the one you see here, and the search tells you: Unit 2, Situation 2.
But type “half past,” and it tells you: that’s not in this course.
So I only need to build the system once, then put the French or Chinese content into it.
For French, the content comes from L’Atelier.
For Chinese, it comes from New Practical Chinese Reader, Book 1.
But how do I decide what goes into the catalogue?
And how do I stop it from becoming too restrictive?
The next two slides answer those questions.

s14.title: Every limit has a source
sentences: How do you build a catalogue?
I use three sources: the textbook, the teacher’s guide and the publisher’s unit tests.
For example, if a unit test asks for something, it counts as taught in that unit.
So whenever I decide that something belongs in a particular unit, I need evidence from one of those three sources.
In other words, I can’t just include something because I happen to know it.
Here are some examples.
“Quarter past” and “half past” aren’t in the French course, because the book tells the time as “nine fifteen” and “nine thirty.” On the other hand, “noon” and “midnight” are in, in Unit 2.
Also, whenever the book introduces a verb, learners practise it with all nine subject pronouns.
And in Chinese, Lesson 11 teaches the time with its own words for “a quarter,” “three quarters” and “half.” So the Chinese course will teach them.
Now, I have to be honest here.
When I checked the first French version against the book, it went way past it.
For instance, twelve colours in the first unit, when the book has two.
“Why” taught four units before the book gets to it.
And a pre-test that marked learners on “half past two,” which the book never teaches.
Every one of those choices seemed helpful at the time.
But learners were being marked on things the course hadn’t taught them.
That’s why I introduced the catalogue.
And from now on, I want the site to check those limits automatically whenever I update it.

s15.title: Seen, Focus, Scored
sentences: Now, you might be thinking: so learners never come across anything new?
In fact, they do.
That’s because the French approach I follow is a spiral.
In a spiral, learners meet things early, as whole phrases, and figure out how they work later.
So I’ve divided what learners encounter into three categories.
Seen means learners come across a phrase, but they don’t have to study it or get tested on it.
Then, Focus means it’s time to learn it properly, with explanations and practice.
And finally, Scored means learners can now be tested on it, but only once the course has taught it.
To picture it, think of a camera.
Something can be in the shot but blurry.
That’s Seen.
Then you bring it into focus.
That’s Focus.
And only then do you take the picture.
That’s Scored.
In practice, learners meet “I was born in” before studying the past tense, and “How are you?” before learning the verb “to go.”
On top of that, I also allow a little unfamiliar language, roughly twenty percent.
That’s because people learn by struggling a bit.
If everything’s familiar, it’s too easy.
If half of it is unknown, it’s too hard.
But learners should never need that unfamiliar language to get the answer right.
To see the difference, look at the first sentence: “At weekends, I go … skiing.” The answer is the word for “some,” so it doesn’t matter that “weekend” is new.
Now the second one says “It is two …” This time, the answer would be “half past,” which is never taught.
So that one’s out.

s16.title: The settings: the key choice moves
sentences: Now for step two, the settings.
This is where French and Chinese start to look quite different.
Here’s the idea: I can keep the same exercise, but change what learners have to choose.
In French, for example, at two stars, the key choice is the article.
You like yoga, so it takes “the.” But you do yoga, so it takes “some.” Look at the two sentences here.
“The” versus “some” is exactly where beginners go wrong, so that’s the gap the learner has to fill.
Mandarin, however, has no articles.
So what goes in the gap?
In this example, it’s the verb that goes with the object.
These all come from the first textbook.
Look at these three examples: play ball, see a film, drink coffee.
So the learner matches each verb to its object.
Another good example is the measure word.
For instance, a piece of clothing takes the classifier you see here.
But the typical beginner mistake is to use the general-purpose one.
So I can reuse the same exercise format, but change the answer depending on the language.
In French, “some” fits and “the” bounces off.
In Chinese, in the same way, the classifier for clothing fits, and the general one bounces off.
Beyond that, Chinese also needs exercises for tones and characters, but these still fit into the same categories.

s17.title: A word never taught, asked once
sentences: There’s another idea I can use in both languages, and I think it could work in others too.
I call it the transfer test.
Here’s how it works.
At the end of an exercise run, I ask learners about a word they’ve never seen before.
In French, for example, the course teaches the masculine and feminine words for “a Chinese person.” Then it asks: what about Luxembourgish?
Nobody taught that one.
But learners know the rule: if the word ends in -s, you add -e.
So they can work out the answer by applying the rule.
You can see it happening here.
However, that answer isn’t marked.
After all, you can’t mark someone wrong on something you never told them.
Instead, the feedback simply gives them the rule.
Chinese works the same way, and the rule’s even simpler: country plus the word for “person” gives you the nationality.
For example, China gives you “a Chinese person.” And Britain gives you “a British person.” Then: Luxembourg?
Same pattern, and here’s the answer.
In the end, that helps me see whether learners have understood the rule or simply memorised the examples.

s18.title: Filling the slots: the teacher writes them
sentences: Now for the third step: filling the slots.
To start, here are the two courses side by side.
French follows L’Atelier: a welcome unit, then four themed units.
You can see their French titles here.
Chinese, meanwhile, follows New Practical Chinese Reader, Book 1, with its fourteen lessons regrouped into five units.
The French book names its situations, adds short workshops built around real documents, which it calls expression workshops, and ends each unit with a Mission.
So for French, I mostly split up and sorted what was already there.
The Chinese book, however, has none of that.
So I have to write the Chinese situations myself.
Twenty-six of them in total.
As for the tasks, lessons 6 and 14 are review lessons, so I use those as the basis for the final tasks.
For the other units, I write the tasks too.
Let me show you what that looks like.

s19.title: When the book gives you nothing: NPCR Lesson 3
sentences: Take New Practical Chinese Reader, Book 1, Lesson 3.
The title is “What country is she from?” The book gives you a text, some notes and pronunciation practice.
But there are no situations, no task, and this lesson doesn’t even have a grammar section.
So I start from what the text actually does.
Look at the first dialogue.
First, someone asks who that is.
The answer: that’s our teacher.
Then: what country is she from?
She’s Chinese.
And then: all our teachers are Chinese.
So from that short dialogue, I can identify two things learners need to do: identify someone and say where they’re from.
Next, the linguistic goals.
First, the verb “to be,” and how to make it negative.

Then the question word “who.” Then the nationality pattern: country plus “person.” And the word “all.” Learners have already seen it in Lesson 2, but they won’t study where it goes in a sentence until Lesson 7.
So for now, they just encounter it, without practising it separately.
Finally, one sound: the negative word changes its tone before a fourth tone.
So “is” and “is not” are said with different tones.
Notice the change here.
As you can see, it’s the same grid as in French.
Only the content is new, and everything comes from the book.
In other words, I keep the same basic structure, but adapt the goals, exercises and situations to Chinese.
And the textbook determines what learners are expected to know.
That’s how the French template becomes a Chinese one.

s20.title: Bonus material and teacher additions
sentences: Still, there are two more categories I need, because textbooks don’t cover everything teachers want to teach.
The first is bonus material: things beyond the book that are still useful.
They’re labelled “bonus” on screen, never marked, and never needed to finish a step.
For example, the book has almost no school subjects, but my students want to introduce themselves.
They want to say things like “I study physics,” in French, as you can see here.
So school subjects stay in, as bonus.
The second category is the teacher addition.
That’s something I choose to teach, even though it isn’t in the textbook.
Unlike bonus material, it’s taught and marked just like book content.
My first example is “pleased to meet you.” The book never teaches it, but I teach it in the very first lesson.
Either way, the catalogue marks each item as either bonus or a teacher addition.
That way, the system knows I’ve included it deliberately, rather than by mistake.

s21.title: AI builds fast. The teacher stays the author.
sentences: A word about how I built this, since the title talks about an AI platform with no development team.
I built FluOLinGo with AI coding tools.
They’re fast, and they made it possible for someone like me, who can’t code.
But they can get the teaching wrong.
Here’s a real example.
Remember the lesson page, with one exercise and three levels?
Earlier AI helpers broke that up into lots of separate activities.
Each looked fine by itself, but the teaching idea behind it was gone, and only a teacher would notice.
Since then, I’ve found two things that help prevent that.
First, I write down my teaching decisions in plain language and make sure the AI always has access to them.
Second, I look at the actual screen myself, because the AI’s description of it can be wrong.
As a result, those written rules help stop the AI from making teaching decisions on its own.
And because every rule comes from a specific source, I can check whether the AI has followed it.
In the same way, you can check my decisions.
In short, it is absolutely necessary that the teacher remains actively in the loop throughout this process.

s22.title: A recipe for your language
sentences: So here’s the recipe, for anyone teaching a less commonly taught language or an Indigenous language.
One.
Start with your textbook.
Identify what learners need to learn, and what they need to be able to do.
Two.
Make a list of exactly what your textbook teaches.
Keep teaching and assessment within those limits, while allowing learners to encounter some new language along the way.
Three.
Give each linguistic goal its own lesson page, and create a few exercise formats you can reuse.
Four.
Write your own situations where your book doesn’t give you any.
No tool can do that part for you.
Five.
One exercise, more levels.
If something’s too easy or too hard, add a level and keep the same screen.
Six.
Write down your decisions and check the actual screens.
Whether you’re working with AI or with a person, the teacher remains the author.
After all, French and Chinese are very different languages.
So if the same approach works for both, that would be a good reason to try it with others.

The French version is live, and planning the Chinese version has given it a new plan too.

So I can’t show you a Chinese screen today.

Can a goal-based platform built for French be adapted for Chinese?
